column4: The section cites this verse: the qibla is turned toward the Sacred Mosque, and “لأتم نعمتي عليكم” joins completion of the gift to finding the way. It gives the path image a concrete communal and bodily direction.

The section’s root ر ب ب gloss includes completing a favor; this verse says “وأتممت عليكم نعمتي” while completing the religion. It makes completion of the gift a whole religious order, not only a material benefit.

The section links completed favor with guidance and response; after washing and purification, this verse says God completes His favor “لعلكم تشكرون.” Its own context connects ritual preparation, purification, and gratitude.
The section cites this verse: the root ن ع م names a favor completed for Joseph and Jacob’s family as it was for Abraham and Isaac. Its family line makes the favored “them” a continuing community.
The section cites Abraham as grateful for God’s favors and guided to a straight path. This verse itself joins “شاكرا لأنعمه” with God’s choosing him and guiding him to “صراط مستقيم.”
The section cites this verse as the joining of Fatiha’s gift and path: “يتم نعمته عليك” and “يهديك صراطا مستقيما.” It states directly that completing the favor includes guidance.
The section cites the command “وأما بنعمة ربك فحدث.” Here the recipient is told to speak of the Lord’s favor, matching its account of hamd as naming a giver’s good before others.
The section cites the Garden-dwellers’ “الحمد لله الذي هدانا لهذا”: their praise names guidance as the gift that brought them there, and they say they would not have been guided without God.
The section cites the final call of the Garden-dwellers, “الحمد لله رب العالمين.” Its return to the exact hamd of 1:2 makes the section’s opening praise recur at the end of the path.

The section cites Moses’ reply “وتلك نعمة تمنها عليّ” to Pharaoh’s claim that he raised him. The verse’s continuation recalls Pharaoh’s enslavement of Israel, exposing a vaunted “favor” against the harm it concealed.

The section’s root ن ع م concerns receiving a benefit; this verse asks a person to thank God for the favor to him and his parents, then to do righteous work. It links reception, gratitude, and a fitting deed.
The section connects receiving favor with hamd; Solomon asks to be grateful for God’s favor to him and his parents and to do righteous work. The verse turns recognition of a gift into conduct.

The section’s dictionary gloss says ن ع م can mean giving beyond measure; Solomon calls the brought throne “من فضل ربي” and treats it as a test of gratitude or denial. The gift tests its recipient’s answer.
The section’s “those You favored” are people on the requested path; this verse names prophets, truthful people, martyrs, and righteous people as those favored by God, identifying that company.

The section’s root ن ع م names God’s favor; this verse forbids people to count their Islam as a favor on the Messenger, then says God favored them by guiding them to faith. It separates the giver’s gift from human self-credit.
The qibla passage just cited completes a favor; here God commands “واشكروا لي ولا تكفرون.” It makes gratitude, rather than denial, the recipient’s answer to divine giving.
The section defines in‘ām as carrying beneficence to another; this verse says God favored believers by sending a Messenger from among them to recite, purify, and teach them.
The section joins favor with the requested straight path; this verse says God guides people through the Book to paths of peace, out of darkness and into light, and to a straight path.
The section links bestowed favor to the recipient’s response; this verse tells the believers to remember when God sheltered, strengthened, and provided good things for them “لعلكم تشكرون.”
The section treats a given good as a favor answered by praise; this verse says to eat lawful, good provision and be grateful for God’s favor if it is Him you worship.

The section describes a favor passed from giver to recipient; this verse says God gave people what they asked for and that His favors cannot be counted, while the human being is unjust and ungrateful.

The section’s root ن ع م names the gift; this repeated Quranic formulation says that if people tried to count God’s favor, they could not enumerate it. It expands the scale of what the receiver owes recognition for.

The section’s dictionary note says the verb can mean “gave more”; this verse promises increase for gratitude and contrasts it with denial. It makes the recipient’s answer affect the abundance of the gift.
The section opens with a dictionary gloss connecting favor and “the hand”; this verse answers the claim that God’s hand is tied with “بل يداه مبسوطتان,” portraying divine giving as open-handed.

The section’s hand-and-favor image is recalled here: believers are told to remember God’s favor when people reached to harm them and God restrained their hands. Its gift is protection from others’ hands.
The section shows a recipient naming beneficence; Moses tells Israel to remember God’s favor when He saved them from Pharaoh’s people, whose oppression the same verse describes.
Moses tells Israel to remember God’s favor: prophets and kings were placed among them and they received what others had not. This makes “those favored” a people with a concrete shared history.
This verse commands believers to remember God’s favor when armies came and He sent wind and unseen forces. It gives a community’s deliverance as another received benefit to recount.

This verse tells believers to remember God’s favor when He joined their hearts after hostility and saved them from the edge of the Fire. Its communal reconciliation shows a favor passed into mutual kinship.

The section connects the straight path with hamd; this verse says believers are guided by their faith to Gardens, where their call is “الحمد لله.” It joins the received path and its praising recipients in one scene.

This verse has the Garden-dwellers praise God for fulfilling His promise and making them inherit the land. It adds the completed promise and received inheritance to the section’s praise at the path’s end.
After Noah and the believers settle in the ship, he is told to say “الحمد لله الذي نجانا.” The verse makes praise a spoken answer for a concrete rescue.
David and Solomon say “الحمد لله” after receiving knowledge and being favored over many believers. Their context exemplifies the section’s recipient recounting the giver’s good.
Abraham praises God for granting him Ishmael and Isaac in old age. The verse makes hamd a public acknowledgment of a specific gift rather than a bare formula.
The section cites 48:2, where completion of favor and straight guidance follow; this preceding verse announces the clear victory that opens that promise’s context.
This verse repeats the command to turn toward the Sacred Mosque, directly continuing the qibla scene that 2:150 connects to completing the favor.

This verse calls prophets “ممن أنعم الله عليهم” and depicts them falling in prostration and weeping when the Merciful’s signs are recited. It identifies favored recipients through their response to revelation.

The section’s path ends with recipients of favor and its wrong alternatives; this verse says God showed the way and that a person may be grateful or ungrateful, explicitly pairing direction with the response.
The section glosses in‘ām as conveying ihsan to another; this verse commands “الإحسان” alongside justice and giving to relatives, stating that beneficence is an enacted duty.
This verse tells Israel to remember the favor God bestowed and His preference for them; the section’s repeated question of who received favor gains a concrete people and a command to name it.
This verse asks people to remember God’s favor and names Him as the creator and provider from heaven and earth. It makes recollection of the giver’s acts concrete.
This verse praises God for sending the Book to His servant, with no crookedness in it. It presents revelation as a given benefit that directs its recipient.
The people of the Garden praise God for removing grief. Their words show hamd as recognition of a completed deliverance, fitting the section’s account of praise after a favor.
The section cites qibla-turning and completed favor in 2:150; this verse speaks of each community’s direction and urges racing toward good, carrying the direction scene into its ethical result.
This verse first commands the Messenger to turn toward the Sacred Mosque; 2:150 returns to that bodily direction and names completion of the favor.
Before the section’s cited praise in 7:43, this verse identifies the Garden’s people as believers who did good. It supplies the deeds and destination behind their thanks for guidance.
After Abraham’s gratitude and guidance in 16:121, this verse says God gave him good in this world and placed him among the righteous in the next. It extends the favor across both lives.
The verse following Abraham’s favor and straight guidance says to follow his upright religion. It makes the recipient’s continued walking on the way explicit.
The section links the favored people with a path; after listing prophets, this verse says they are those God guided and commands the Messenger to follow their guidance.
The section says the favor is completed by walking the path; here those who strive for God are promised guidance to His ways. It links effort on the way with further guidance.
The section opens from “الرحمن الرحيم” as a source of kindness; this verse calls the Messenger “رحمة للعالمين,” making mercy itself a benefit carried to others.
The section’s lexicon defines in‘ām as delivering beneficence to another; this verse uses the same root for God’s favor to Zayd and the Prophet’s favor to him, in a concrete human relationship.
The section’s image is a favor received and answered; Abraham asks God to provide fruits for his family near the Sacred House “لعلهم يشكرون,” explicitly linking provision to gratitude.
This verse says sacrificial animals were made subject so people may mention God’s name over them and eat from them. It gives a concrete provided good and a spoken acknowledgment.

The verse says neither flesh nor blood reaches God, but piety does, and that He subjected the animals so believers glorify Him for guidance. It separates the gift from the recipient’s fitting response.
David’s family are told to work in gratitude for what they were given. This makes thanks an active return of benefit, not only words.
When people settle on mounts, this verse tells them to remember their Lord’s favor and say “سبحان الذي سخر لنا هذا.” It joins an ordinary benefit, its source, and public praise.
The section’s secondary dictionary gloss says أنعم can mean doing more and increasing; this verse pictures a gift in God’s way multiplied many times over, making increase part of the image of giving.
This verse says whatever good is spent benefits the spenders, provided they seek God’s face; it locates the giver’s intention and reward rather than turning a gift into a social debt.
The section’s definition of in‘ām is conveying beneficence to another; this verse connects righteousness with spending what one loves, giving a concrete cost to that transfer of good.
This verse describes those who spend in ease and hardship, restrain anger, and pardon people as benefactors God loves. It gives the section’s conveyed ihsan concrete forms.
The section’s lexicon glosses favor through “اليد”; this verse orders the giving of due to relatives, the poor, and travelers, showing the hand’s benefit reaching others.
The section describes a gift passing from giver to recipient; this verse depicts feeding the needy, orphan, and captive despite one’s own desire for the food.
The section treats a gift as answered by a fitting path; this verse begins the paired paths with giving and God-consciousness, followed by belief in the best.
The same passage names belief in “الحسنى” after giving and piety; this verse supplies the recipient’s trust that frames the ease promised next.
The generous, believing person is “فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْيُسْرَى”; the section’s link between completing a favor and walking a path is here expressed as being eased toward ease.
This verse commands gratitude to God and parents, grounding the received favor in a parent’s care and naming gratitude as the response.
This verse points to fruit made available for people to eat and asks whether they will not be grateful. It turns a concrete provision into the recipient’s answer.
The sea is made subject for food, ornaments, ships, and seeking bounty; the verse ends by asking whether people will be grateful. It gives the section’s gift-and-response relation a concrete scene.
God makes night and day so people may rest and seek His bounty, yet many are ungrateful. This verse connects an everyday provision to its often-missing acknowledgment.
The sea is subjected so ships may sail and people seek God’s bounty and give thanks. It repeats the section’s relation between a provided good and its response.
This verse promises multiplied return and noble reward to charitable men and women. It resonates with the section’s secondary gloss of the verb as giving more and increasing.
The section’s secondary dictionary form says the act may exceed and increase; this verse gives tenfold return for a good deed, a specific Quranic image of good being augmented.
This verse promises that whoever comes with a good deed will receive better than it. It offers a concrete counterpart to the section’s dictionary sense of exceeding one’s deed.

This verse says God has favored some people over others in provision, while those favored do not return their provision equally to those under their authority. It puts unequal gift and human reciprocity in view.
This verse names God’s honoring of the children of Adam, carrying them, providing good things, and favoring them over many creatures. It makes the favor’s material and dignifying forms explicit.
This verse names God’s outward and inward favors upon people, then notes their dispute without knowledge. It connects the section’s gift with both visible and hidden forms of benefit.
This verse asks whether people will be grateful if God made their drinking water bitter after describing the water they drink. It makes a specific life-sustaining gift the subject of gratitude.
The verse calls fire a reminder and provision for travelers after describing its creation. It names another concrete benefit that recipients can recognize.
After describing fire and provision, this verse commands glorifying the name of the Lord Most Great. It places praise immediately after a given benefit.
This verse says guidance is God’s responsibility, setting the source of direction behind the two paths and their different outcomes in the surrounding passage.
The verse says both the first life and the Hereafter belong to God, widening the two-path passage’s horizon beyond immediate ease or hardship.

The section distinguishes telling a giver’s goodness from vaunting it; this verse praises spending that is followed by neither reminder nor injury. It marks the boundary between beneficence and turning it into a debt.

The section’s hamd names a giver’s goodness; this verse says a kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury. It shows how speech can preserve kindness when a gift might otherwise humiliate.

The section’s source gloss for ح م د includes “يتحمد علي,” reminding someone of one’s favor. This verse forbids invalidating charity by reminders and injury, and compares ostentatious giving to a bare rock after rain.
The section’s root ن ع م names a received favor; this verse says people recognize God’s favor and then deny it. That is the explicit reversal of acknowledging the giver.
This verse says open charity is good while concealing it for the poor is better. It clarifies that public visibility alone is not the same as the section’s vaunting of a favor.
The section’s hand image meets a limit here: the verse warns against keeping one’s hand chained or extending it without restraint. It bounds giving so that beneficence remains sustainable.
The verse explains that feeding is “لوجه الله” and seeks neither repayment nor thanks. It contrasts freely given kindness with reminding a recipient of one’s favor.
The counter-path begins with withholding and self-sufficiency, opposing the section’s image of benefit extended from one hand to another.
This verse adds denial of “الحسنى” to the withholding person’s path, a direct contrary answer to receiving and recognizing good.
The verse says such a person will be eased toward hardship, reversing the guidance and completion associated with the section’s favored path.

The section’s root ن ع م names a favor that is completed; this verse says God does not change a favor bestowed on a people until they change what is within themselves. It sets a boundary on its continuance.
The section’s recipient answers a favor with hamd; this verse says a person turns aside when favored, the contrary response that exposes ingratitude.
After a favor follows hardship, this verse depicts a person boasting and exulting instead of acknowledging the giver. It is a specific reversal of hamd as the recipient’s answer.
This verse says a person forgets the prayer he made in distress once given a favor, then assigns partners to God. It shows benefit answered by forgetfulness rather than praise.
After receiving a favor, the person says “I was given it because of knowledge”; the verse calls the gift a test. It exposes self-credit in place of recognizing the giver.
When favored, the person turns away and distances himself; when harmed, he makes lengthy supplication. This reverses the section’s recipient who names the giver’s good.
This verse says people rejoice when given a taste of mercy but despair when evil touches them. It offers a specific, unstable response to benefit in place of settled hamd.
When people taste mercy, they rejoice, but when harm reaches them for what their hands did, they are ungrateful. The verse names the opposite answer to a received favor.

A person reads abundant provision as “my Lord honored me”; the following verses challenge that inference and condemn failure to honor the orphan. It tests whether material favor is met with care for others.
The paired verse treats restricted provision as humiliation, an inference the passage rejects. It warns against equating outward condition with the giver’s judgment of a person.
The verse challenges the prior claims about abundance and restriction by asking why people do not honor the orphan. It redirects attention from status to beneficence toward another.
When hardship touches people they call on God, then some associate others with Him after tasting mercy. The verse gives a communal reversal of recognizing the giver.
The section’s root ن ع م names a favor; this repeated question asks which of the Lord’s favors jinn and humans deny, following descriptions of created order and provision.
The section asks who receives favor; this verse opens Israel’s covenant address with “اذكروا نعمتي” and calls them to remember the favor God bestowed, making the recipient community explicit.
This repeated address again tells Israel to remember the favor God bestowed and His preference for them. It confirms the section’s collective “those favored” through a recurring Quranic formulation.
The verse tells believers to remember God’s favor and their covenant with Him. It ties recollection of beneficence to keeping faith with its giver.

Following the qibla passage cited by the section, this verse describes the Messenger reciting, purifying, and teaching believers what they did not know; the next verse commands gratitude. It continues the scene of guidance as a given benefit.
The section’s source gloss for ح م د includes reminding another of one’s favor; this verse commands “ولا تمنن تستكثر,” forbidding a gift given with a reminder or expectation of more in return.
These people vow that if God gives them from His bounty, they will give charity and be righteous. The verse begins a concrete test of whether received favor is answered with generosity.
After they receive the promised bounty, they withhold it and turn away. This is a specific reversal of the section’s recipient who answers beneficence by acknowledging the giver.
The passage says their broken promise and lying leave hypocrisy in their hearts. It shows the lasting consequence of refusing the response owed after a favor.
In the passage about the Ansar welcoming those who migrated to them, this verse says they prefer others over themselves despite need. It depicts benefit passed freely from one hand to another.
The section defines in‘ām as carrying ihsan to another; this verse commands, “وأحسن كما أحسن الله إليك,” directly making God’s beneficence the pattern for human beneficence.
This passage calls the moral way a steep ascent, then describes freeing and feeding as how it is crossed. It concretely joins the section’s gift and its claim that completion comes by walking a path.
The first act on the “steep ascent” is freeing a person from bondage, a specific human good that makes the path of beneficence concrete.
The next act on the ascent is feeding on a day of hunger, directly depicting a good delivered from one person to another.
The feeding is directed to an orphan who is a relative, specifying a vulnerable recipient of the kindness.
The passage continues with feeding a needy person in hardship, completing its account of beneficence toward others.
After freeing and feeding, the passage names faith, mutual counsel to patience, and mutual counsel to mercy. It joins deeds of care to the path’s communal continuation.
The passage concludes that these are the companions of the right, giving the recipients of the path a concrete identity.
The verse says those invoked besides God cannot provide, then commands people to seek provision from God, worship Him, and give thanks: “واشكروا له.” It joins the giver, the gift, and its answer.
This verse states “وما بكم من نعمة فمن الله”: every favor people have comes from God. It makes the giver’s hand behind each received benefit explicit.
After God removes their harm, a group associates others with Him. The continuation shows a received benefit answered by denial rather than hamd.
The Messenger is told to say that people should rejoice in God’s bounty and mercy, better than what they accumulate. It gives public acknowledgment of divine beneficence a positive form.
This verse calls God’s bounty to people and says most do not give thanks. It repeats the section’s relation between the giver’s good and the recipient’s response.
The verse says the Lord has bounty toward people but most are not grateful, a repeated formulation of favor meeting an inadequate response.
After describing the two seas, this verse names food, adornment, ships, and seeking bounty, then says people may give thanks. It gives the benefit-and-response pattern a concrete scene.
The verse asks what God would do with people’s punishment if they are grateful and believe. It makes gratitude the meaningful answer from the recipient, not a benefit God needs.
Noah is described as a grateful servant after the verse recalls those carried with him. It supplies another specific recipient whose response is gratitude for deliverance.
The verse pictures lending God a good loan that He multiplies many times over, echoing the section’s secondary dictionary sense of giving more and increasing.
Whoever lends God a good loan will have it multiplied and receive a noble reward. It repeats the image of a given good returning enlarged.
This verse says a good loan to God will be multiplied and forgiven, another explicit Quranic formulation of beneficence returned in greater measure.
The verse says whatever people spend, God replaces it and is the best provider. It connects a person’s giving to the prior and continuing source of provision.

Those who spend by night and day, privately and publicly, are promised their reward with God. It develops the section’s concern with speaking or acting publicly while locating the reward with the giver.
The section begins from “الرحمن الرحيم” as the source of kindness; this verse opens with “الرحمن,” carrying that named source of beneficence into a passage about provision and teaching.
Immediately after naming the Merciful, this verse says He taught the Quran. It makes guidance itself a beneficence that comes from the mercy at the section’s beginning.
This verse calls the Quran healing and mercy for believers. It connects revelation and guidance to the section’s claim that mercy is the source of good.
After Adam’s story, God promises that guidance will come and says whoever follows it will have no fear or grief. It specifies the path as a received gift and the consequence of walking it.
Before the section’s cited guidance in 5:16, this verse says a light and clear Book have come from God. It supplies the revelation through which the next verse guides people.
God expands the breast of the one He guides to Islam and makes the one He leaves constricted. It portrays guidance as a received opening and its opposite as a boundary.
This verse names “صراطي مستقيما,” commands following it, and forbids following diverging paths. It gives the section’s straight path and its excluded alternatives a precise formulation.
The verse describes people who prefer worldly life, turn others from God’s path, and seek to make it crooked. It is a specific contrary stance to the straight path of those favored.
Every nation is shown a Messenger calling to worship God; some are guided and some persist in error. This explicitly stages the two outcomes beside the section’s favored path.
The Quran is said to guide to what is most upright and give believers good news. It presents revealed guidance as a benefit that directs its recipient toward the way.
The verse promises that whoever follows God’s guidance will neither stray nor be miserable. It states what walking the received path does for its recipient.
The next verse describes the one who turns away from God’s remembrance as living a constricted life. It names the contrary outcome to following the guidance in 20:123.
The parable ends by saying God guides to His light whom He wills. Its light image gives a concrete metaphor for receiving direction from God.
The verse says God guides whom He wills and knows those who are guided. It clarifies that the path’s source is the giver, not the recipient’s control.
The revelation is called a light by which God guides whom He wills, and the verse names a straight path. It joins received revelation, divine guidance, and the section’s path image.
The verse says the Messenger has been placed upon a clear way and commands him to follow it rather than the desires of those without knowledge. It stages the path and its alternative.
Those who are guided are increased in guidance and given their piety. It extends the section’s link between receiving a favor and continuing to walk its way.
God makes faith beloved in believers’ hearts and disbelief hateful, then identifies them as rightly guided through “فضلا من الله ونعمة.” It names inwardly given faith as favor and guidance.
The verse promises two portions of mercy and a light by which believers walk. It makes the section’s movement from mercy to a path people can travel explicit.
The Messenger recites clear signs to bring believers from darkness into light, and those who believe enter Gardens. It depicts revelation as the gift that leads along the way.
God invites to the Home of Peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path. It directly links the destination, the giver’s invitation, and guidance on the way.
The verse identifies successful people as those who believe in the Messenger and follow the light sent down with him. It makes following revealed guidance the recipient’s continued step on the path.
God brings believers from darkness into light, while the allies of disbelievers bring them from light into darkness. It gives the path’s guided and contrary directions a specific boundary.
God and His angels bless believers to bring them from darkness into light, and He is merciful to them. It joins mercy and guidance as gifts given to the community.
The verse says God directs people to the straight path, while some turn aside from it; had He willed, He could have guided all. It states both guidance and deviation as possible responses.
Clear signs are sent down, and God guides whom He wills to a straight path. It repeats the connection between revealed signs and the path’s divine source.
God makes chosen servants leaders who guide by His command and inspires them to do good, prayer, and almsgiving. It combines a given role, a way, and beneficent action.
After patience, some are made leaders guiding by God’s command. It supplies another concrete group whose path is both received and walked.
After the wrongdoers are cut off, this verse says “الحمد لله رب العالمين.” It repeats hamd as the spoken acknowledgment after a completed divine act.
